entry.title: [sahandiranmehr] What do 23 votes in favor and 3 votes against mean? Sahand Iranmehr. Numbers…
entry.summary:
Source: @sahandiranmehr

What do 23 votes in favor and 3 votes against mean? Sahand Iranmehr. Numbers are tantalizing because they evoke a sense of undeniable decisiveness and certainty, but the famous saying "statistics speak" is not entirely true, at least in political analysis. The 23 votes in favor, 3 votes against, and 8 abstentions show that Iran has been left in the minority at the IAEA Board of Governors and a resolution against it has been passed. The meaning of these statistics is that the majority of the Board of Governors has not sided with Iran's position. This fact should not be downplayed, nor should one, for instance, flaunt the negative votes of China, Russia, and Niger to compensate. However, at the same time, this vote does not mean that the matter is over and that new sanctions, this time from the United Nations, are on the way. It is true that the Board of Governors can report the case to the Security Council, but the Security Council has its own specific rules, because now Russia and China, in addition to their negative votes, are permanent members with veto power. Just as Iran being in the minority there was a bitter reality, here in the Security Council, one should not romanticize the negative votes of Moscow, Beijing, and Niger either, considering the veto right. The negative votes of Russia, China, and Niger do not mean that they endorse all of Iran's nuclear policies or consider the differences between Tehran and the Agency to be fabricated. They oppose the politicized process of dealing with Iran's nuclear issue, a path that seeks to drag the case to the Security Council more than it serves the Agency's goals. This is also why China and Russia, despite being in the minority in Vienna, see their minority status fade in New York where the veto power works. If we want to face the issue realistically, we must accept that 23 votes in favor are, in any case, a serious wake-up call, and even if it is proven to be a political move, the essence of the issue does not change. Nevertheless, the West is also far from a complete victory. Taking the case from Vienna to New York is one thing, and obtaining a binding decision in the Security Council is another. The majority formed today in the Board of Governors will not necessarily be repeated in the Security Council, but how far this organized effort based on global consensus will continue, how far the brakes of China and Russia will work, or how far other variables will keep these two aligned with Iran, is something that, in a wise approach, one cannot gamble on too much. @sahandiranmehr

entry.title: [sahandiranmehr] The World of Retribution Does the world have a reckoning? Do people eventually…
entry.summary:
Source: @sahandiranmehr

The World of Retribution
Does the world have a reckoning? Do people eventually see the consequences of what they do to others? Is the world truly a place of retribution, and should one never be heedless of the consequences of one's actions?

In this episode, we turn to a tale from the book "Al-Faraj Ba'd al-Shiddah" by "Tanukhi": the story of a man who, at the height of his power, imprisons another and threatens him with the whip, only to later fall into the hands of that very same structure of power.

This episode explores the difference between a just world and a world where human actions have consequences, yet there is no guarantee that justice will be served.

entry.title: [sahandiranmehr] ✔️New game and new toys ✍🏻 Sahand Iranmehr. This new wave of ethnic…
entry.summary:
Source: @sahandiranmehr

✔️New game and new toys ✍🏻 Sahand Iranmehr. This new wave of ethnic content — from conferences, interviews, and articles to posts and tweets — that has surged across social media over the past few days, if traced back to its origins and background, leads to the same group that, before the time of the aggression, had as their refrain "Free Iran," and we saw how the disgrace of their failed "Iran-selling" deal came crashing down, as acknowledged by the parties to the deal. Now, it seems the bargaining for a new deal has secretly begun; with the difference that this time the veil is thinner, and the language is more overt and more ethnicist. Follow any of these threads, and you'll either reach an Israeli outlet or a message from a minister or lawyer attributed to that same ethnicity, who, as before, incites their pawns and followers with the promise of "we will support you"; as if for this final act, they've polished the tambourine and drum anew and tuned a fresh instrument. Before this war, those lovers of the homeland who warned that the "Iran, Iran" chanting of this lot was but diluted yogurt sold as grape syrup, their frothing mouths of insolence would not pause for a moment to brand and shame; but time showed they had neither a passion for Iran nor for Iranians. This time too, neither freedom is their concern, nor even the ethnicity whose self-appointed advocates and spokespeople they claim to be. The issue is something else entirely, and all this theatrical black play, despite all the differences in slogans, guise, roles, and craft in phrasing, if they converge on one point, that point is the destruction of what is the common heritage of us all: Iran. Iran is neither the property of one ethnicity nor the privilege of one group; it is the historic home of peoples whose similarities and differences, side by side for centuries, have forged the meaning of Iran, and any hand that tears this bond apart in the name of ethnicity, language, or religion, before separating another from Iran, has already destroyed a part of Iran itself. Playing with ethnic divides, whatever name it gives itself and whatever flag it raises — if its end result is the weakening of this bond and the ruin of the homeland, as they have shown it to be — is not freedom, but rather the renewed game of the behind-the-scenes homeless with the very foundation of the home and hearth in which all of us Iranians have a share. @sahandiranmehr

entry.title: [sahandiranmehr] Being anti-Iran is no longer just about someone waving Trump's flag or sharing…
entry.summary:
Source: @sahandiranmehr

Being anti-Iran is no longer just about someone waving Trump's flag or sharing his intentions; any move, with any intention and under any guise, that aligns with Trump's policies against Iran, whether it rejoices in their realization or gives them leeway, is anti-Iranian at a strategic level. Reducing this situation to merely being against the Islamic Republic is either self-deception or demagoguery. When Trump tears away a new veil every day of what he wants for Iran, one can no longer fail to see this alignment, even in a single area, as anti-Iranian. Intention does not erase responsibility for the consequences. @sahandiranmehr

[sahandiranmehr] ✔️ A dream that returned to die Written by: Sahand Iranmehr
Eurydice had…
entry.summary:
Source: @sahandiranmehr

✔️ A dream that returned to die
Written by: Sahand Iranmehr

Eurydice had died once. Orpheus was allowed to bring her back from the underworld; but right at the threshold of freedom, he looked back and lost her forever. Sometimes history's plan for those whose fate is tied to an inevitable death is exactly this: it gives a dead thing a chance to return—not to revive it, but so that its death becomes final this time.

Perhaps "57" was not an absolute end for the monarchy—or whatever other name was later given to it; it was a historical wound whose final fate could still be doubted. But if today some supporters of that dream have pinned their hopes on Israel's attack and its plans for Iran—from partition to nuclear threats, with Trump as a hired hand—to bring it back, and to realize this dream they are forced to stand ever more openly, recklessly, and violently alongside this project, they may, just like Orpheus, realize at the very moment they think they have found a chance at life again that they themselves have sealed the absolute death of the idea of monarchy and kingship in the minds of Iranians.

Then "57" will no longer be just the date of the monarchy's fall; it could become the moment when the idea of monarchy, after a second chance, lost the possibility of return forever.

Orpheus lost Eurydice once more because he looked back right at the brink of her revival. Perhaps some political dreams are like that too: they fail once, but they get a second chance not to return, but to die for good.

Sometimes an idea does not die from its first crushing defeat and blow, but from the way its followers choose to resurrect it.

Artwork description:
"Orpheus and Eurydice," an 1864 oil painting by the British artist Sir Frederic Leighton
@sahandiranmehr

entry.title: [sahandiranmehr] ✔️Returning to the homeland and fear of a rift in the opposition!…
entry.summary:
Source: @sahandiranmehr

✔️Returning to the homeland and fear of a rift in the opposition! ✍🏻Sahand Iranmehr
The return of an Iranian who has not taken up arms against his country, has not called for violence, and has not supported foreign aggression against Iran should, in principle, be a matter of course—not a political concession. If even a modicum of rationality were applied, thousands of compatriots at home who harbor the unavoidable dream of emigration could also stay put.
That the trouble-free return of a handful of compatriots today comes as a surprise to some is the result of conditions that have driven a wedge between the Iranian and his homeland—a wedge that has provided the perfect ecosystem for all kinds of crises to take root and, consequently, for those who profit from them to thrive. So if this fledgling and "still trembling sapling of return" is displeasing to some, it may be because they would rather not see even a single knot in this tangled skein of "Iran's situation" come undone. It is these knots, piled one upon another, that absolve reason from effort, keep the cauldron of rage simmering on its own, and turn blood into a commodity for trade and for garnering support among this lot.
If the fly flees the dunghill, these too abhor conflict and prefer union over separation; because in their view, if a knot is to be untied, it must first receive the blessing of a Homa's shadow, and portraits must dance upon the shoulders of rage and destruction, and a brother must hide a blade in his sleeve aimed at the jugular of his own kin; for in a politics built on elimination, reconciliation and return are sometimes more dangerous than defeat itself, and they stoke the fires of crisis more than ever.
In short, don't be too surprised if they say: "These permissions are meant to create a rift in the opposition!" And don't be astonished if, one distant day, when the Homa's shadow falls upon the nation and the bitter times have passed, this lost lot mourns the dissipation of the opposition and beats their heads in despair!
These returns are, of course, good; even better is when all these differences and even hair-pulling squabbles take place within Iran, under the red line of "Iran." But sit back and watch how, in the days ahead, the knife and cheese—both inside and outside, with seemingly opposing edges—will secretly join hands to stitch the earth to the sky for this trembling, fledgling endeavor. Freeing Iran from its troubles has long since, for some, ceased to be a struggle for change and become a furnace to fan the flames within; and that is how, instead of thinking about solving its problems, they think about keeping them unsolved—and we've seen that if they catch wind of a "Truman Plus" that could wrap things up, they'll cheer for that too.
@sahandiranmehr
